title: Not Every Decision Deserves Your Evening
author: Andrea Chiarelli
source: The Art of Asking Questions (andreachiarelli.substack.com), October 25, 2026
summary: Andrea Chiarelli, a consultant used to making decisions by a Thursday deadline, argues that most people have the opposite problem and lose hours to choices that do not matter, like which film to watch or which restaurant to pick. The assumption doing the damage, she says, is that difficult means important, when a choice can feel hard because the options are close, incomparable or simply under-informed. She borrows three quick tests from Annie Duke's How to Decide: the Happiness Test (will I remember this in a week, a month, a year), the Only-Option Test (would I be happy with each option if it were the only one), and the two-way door test (can I undo it). Passing any one of them means a decision can be made fast, with the caveat that recurring choices should be judged as patterns rather than instances. Drawing on philosopher Ruth Chang, she reserves the evening, the weekend and the long walk for choices where the options are on a par and the decision is really about what you will care about.
points: Chiarelli's key reframe is that difficulty tells you nothing about importance, so a hard-feeling choice between close options is evidence that you can afford to go fast.
Duke's HOT shortcut (Happiness, Only-option, Two-way door) gives a concrete triage: any one pass means decide quickly, and a flip of the coin is acceptable when both options would satisfy you.
Over-research persists because it buys a defence against being judged on outcomes, what Duke calls resulting, rather than because it improves the choice.
The speed rule has limits: irreversible choices keep their weight, and repeated choices like weekday dinners should be judged as patterns.
Ruth Chang's on-a-par decisions, such as money against meaning, cannot be solved with more information and deserve real time because they are settled by deciding what you will care about.
quotes: The assumption doing most of the damage is that difficult means important. If a choice seems difficult, we consider that as evidence that something is at stake, and that there is some ‘right’ answer that will surface if we read one more review or try on one more shirt.
The choice felt heavy because you were inside it, and the middle of a decision is a terrible vantage point from which to judge its size.
If the answer is yes both times, you are done, and the only thing you can reasonably do is to flip a coin. Because it can’t land on an outcome that disappoints you.
The very thing that is slowing you down, which is how close the options are, is the proof that you can afford to go fast. Whichever one you pick, you cannot be far wrong.

So, the over-researching is not irrational at all, even though it’s not necessary from the point of view of effective decision-making. It is our insurance policy against a verdict that will be coming independently of we do.
Can I undo this? Where the answer is yes, speed costs almost nothing. Where the answer is no, the closeness of the options should not be interpreted as a licence to hurry.

Chang’s conclusion is that these choices cannot be settled by finding out more, since there is no further fact waiting to be found. They are settled by deciding what you are going to care about, which takes as long as it takes and is not a failure of decisiveness when it takes months.
